title: Image Classification on IBM Quantum Computers
authors: Junghoon Justin Park, Jiook Cha, Jun-gyeong Park, Hwidong Yoo, Kwangmin Yu
abstract: Quantum machine learning on real noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware has remained largely confined to binary or few-class tasks, limited by the cost of on-hardware training and the underuse of large devices at inference. We present a unified framework that classifies ten-class MNIST end-to-end on a $127$-qubit IBM Eagle processor, with three central contributions. First, a two-phase protocol decouples a gradient-based classical optimization of the encoder and readout from a gradient-free optimization of the quantum parameters, removing the parameter-shift gradient cost that makes on-hardware training impractical. Second, we introduce Quantum Multi-Programming to a trained quantum classifier for the first time, packing multiple circuit copies onto one device to deliver parallel inference at no mean-accuracy cost while cutting quantum-processor job submissions proportionally. Third, a controlled comparison shows that on-hardware fine-tuning yields no measurable accuracy gain, motivating a practical NISQ workflow: train on a classical simulator and reserve the hardware for inference only. Benchmarked against a matched-capacity classical network, the quantum module shows no per-parameter accuracy advantage at this scale; we therefore frame the work as a feasibility-and-workflow demonstration for multi-class quantum image classification on current hardware.
summary: This paper demonstrates a practical workflow for running multi-class image classification using variational quantum circuits on current NISQ hardware. By proposing a two-phase training protocol and implementing Quantum Multi-Programming, the authors significantly boost inference throughput while concluding that classical simulation should handle training, reserving expensive hardware time only for forward passes.
main_problem: The primary challenge is demonstrating a feasible, high-throughput workflow for multi-class Quantum Machine Learning (QML) on current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware.
main_result: The authors established an 'inference-only' workflow: training classically and reserving the quantum processor solely for inference. They achieved significant throughput gains using Quantum Multi-Programming without sacrificing accuracy.
method: A two-phase hybrid protocol was used, decoupling classical optimization from gradient-free quantum parameter optimization (COBYLA). Inference efficiency was boosted by packing multiple circuit copies onto one job submission.
model_or_system: The work uses a variational quantum classifier applied to the ten-class MNIST dataset on an IBM 127-qubit Eagle processor. The model architecture is a hybrid classical-quantum structure utilizing a VQC ZigZag ansatz.
key_observables: Classification accuracy (compared to classical MLP), end-to-end wall time/throughput, and circuit metrics like depth and CNOT count.
important_parameters: The system size involves 12 qubits ($n_q=12$) for the quantum module. The key operational parameters are the packing factor $K$ (e.g., $K=4$).
main_assumptions: The work assumes that training on hardware is prohibitively expensive and yields no measurable accuracy benefit over simulator training, thus necessitating an inference-only workflow.
figures_summary: Figure 3 illustrates the flat optimization loss during Phase 2 (quantum parameter tuning), showing no movement in classification decisions when switching from simulation to hardware. Other figures detail circuit structures and performance metrics for varying $K$.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of identifying limitations (training cost, low throughput) $ightarrow$ proposing novel protocols (two-phase training, QMP) $ightarrow$ validating the workflow on real hardware $ightarrow$ concluding that classical simulation/hardware inference separation is the practical path forward.
why_interesting: While focused on ML, the core technical contributions—decoupling optimization steps and maximizing device utilization via multi-programming—are highly relevant to developing robust quantum algorithms for near-term devices.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Logical VQC ZigZag circuit (nq = 12, L = 3): a Y -axis angle embedding (RY ) of the encoder output, then L layers of single-qubit RX, RY , RZ rotations and two brick-wall CRX sublayers (even then odd adjacent pairs, no wrap-around), and a Pauli-Z readout on all 12 qubits. Gate labels are symbolic rather than numerical: zi is the encoder output angle applied to qubit i (twelve distinct, sample-dependent values), and θ(ℓ) RX, θ(ℓ) RY , θ(ℓ) RZ, θ(ℓ) CRX,even, θ(ℓ) CRX,odd are the five trainable angles of layer ℓ; the figure carries the layer index as a subscript and abbreviates the even- and odd-pair sublayers as e and o. Each angle is shared across all twelve qubits of its layer,...

Fig. 2: Pinned physical-qubit layout on the ibm yonsei heavy-hex topology (high- lighted = active). (a) K = 1 runs use Circuit 1; (b) K = 4 QMP concatenates four routing-disconnected 12-qubit circuits with no inter-circuit coupling. Circuit 1 (the K = 1 layout) is reused as the first of the four circuits.

Fig. 3: Two-phase training curves for VQC ZigZag (12q/3L, MNIST 350/75/75; mean ± s.d. over three seeds). Phase 1 (Adam, 30 epochs, classical layers) raises validation accuracy to ∼78%, while Phase 2 (COBYLA, 20 epochs, quantum parameters) is essentially flat in every cell. The red dashed line marks the Aer →hardware switch at Phase 2 epoch 19 for the hybrid-trained Cells 4–5. The flat Phase 2 traces visualize the central result of Claim 3: gradient-free quantum-parameter optimization, whether on a simulator or on hardware, does not move the classification decisions.
